Er, he said Sub-Saharan. And from looking at the article, he actually seems to be right. Northern Africa had a few indigenous writing systems, but mostly used the Arabic and Phoenician systems of their conquerors. The few Southern African writing systems that are mentioned are very recent inventions (as recent as the 70s) which I'd be willing to bet would not have been possible without Western education.

Sub Saharan includes 90% of Africa, the only parts excluded are on the northern coast. Three written languages developed in the sub Saharan region. Tifinagh, Ge'ez, and Nsibidi.

The Tifinagh alphabet is still actively used to varying degrees in trade and modernized forms for writing of Berber languages (Tamazight, Tamashek, etc.) of the Maghreb, Sahara, and Sahel regions.

The Ge'ez script is an abugida that was developed in the Horn of Africa for writing the Ge'ez language. The script is used today in Ethiopia and Eritrea for Amharic, Tigrinya, Tigre, and several other languages. It is sometimes called Ethiopic, and is known in Ethiopia as the fidel or abugida

Nsibidi (also known as "nsibiri", "nchibiddi", and "nchibiddy") is a system of symbols indigenous to what is now southeastern Nigeria that is apparently an ideographic script, though there have been suggestions that it includes logographic elements. The symbols are at least several centuries old: Early forms appeared on excavated pottery as well as what are most likely ceramic stools and headrests from the Calabar region, with a range of dates from 400 to 1400 CE.

I will concede that the first example "The Tifinagh alphabet" has mixed origins from both sub Saharan and Arabic cultures but it still has roots in sub Saharan regions.
